entry.title: Onyema v Commonwealth of Australia (as represented by the Australian Taxation Office) (extension of time, application for stay) [2026] FCA 1530
entry.content:
Kenneth Onyema sought judicial review of the ATO’s decision to terminate his APS employment for unauthorised access to taxation records. In this interlocutory judgment, the Federal Court held that he did not need an extension of time, refused a stay of the termination decision, granted leave to amend, and fixed the proper respondents.

Key holding: Under s 11(1)(c) of the ADJR Act, an application for review is “lodged” when it comes into the possession of the Registry or its staff, not when it is later accepted and filed, so receipt within the prescribed period satisfies the time limit.

An application for review will be "lodged" when it comes into the possession of a Registry or a staff of a Registry: EIW20 at [67], quoting Hong v Minister for Immigration and Multicultural Affairs [1998] FCA 341; (1998) 82 FCR 468 at 471 (the Court).

entry.title: LFQR and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social security second review) [2026] ARTA 2320
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a refusal to pay family tax benefit top ups and supplements for 2022/23 because the applicant’s partner lodged his income tax return on 4 July 2024, after the 30 June 2024 reconciliation deadline. The applicant relied on stress, family violence, alcohol issues, a brief separation and pandemic-related pressures. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal, finding no special circumstances that prevented the partner from lodging on time.

Key holding: Under s 32D(1)(c)(ii) of the Administration Act, special circumstances will only extend the reconciliation time if they actually prevented the partner from lodging the income tax return by the required date.

For the Applicant to be paid top ups and supplements of family tax benefit for 2022/23, the Tribunal must be satisfied that there are special circumstances that prevented the Applicant's partner from lodging his income tax return by 30 June 2024.

entry.title: Hui and Commissioner of Taxation (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2319
entry.content:
The applicant sought review of several Taxation Office decisions concerning his income tax affairs, including invalid objection determinations. The Tribunal found it had no jurisdiction because the decisions were not reviewable objection decisions under s 14ZQ of the Taxation Administration Act 1953 (Cth). The application was dismissed.

Key holding: A decision that is not a reviewable objection decision within s 14ZQ of the Taxation Administration Act 1953 (Cth) is not reviewable by the Tribunal under s 14ZZA, so the Tribunal lacks jurisdiction.

I have had due regard to the decisions submitted by the applicant and find that they are not reviewable objection decisions within the meaning of section 14ZQ of the Taxation Administration Act 1953 (Cth) and, accordingly, the Tribunal has no jurisdiction under section 14ZZA to review them.

entry.title: Ms Mary Muzorewa v Eldercare Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 3623
entry.content:

The Commission considered whether to extend time under s.366(2) but found no exceptional circumstances, largely because her reliance on ANMF/administrative processes did not reasonably explain the delay. Key holding: The Commission may extend time for a s.365 general protections dismissal application under s.366(2) only if satisfied that exceptional circumstances exist, taking into account the statutory factors.

Section 366(2) of the Act provides the Commission with discretion to extend the time for lodgement beyond the 21 -day period where it is satisfied that exceptional circumstances exist to warrant that action. In considering whether exceptional circumstances exist for this purpose, I am required to take into account the considerations outlined in paragraphs (a) to (e) of s.366(2) of the Act.

entry.title: Community Accommodation and Respite Agency Incorporated v United Workers Union & Australian Services Union (ASU) [2026] FWC 3878
entry.content:
CARA referred a dispute under s.739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 concerning cl 6.11 of the CARA Support Employees Enterprise Agreement 2022. The Commission determined whether employees who agree to supervise clients on overnight excursions, camps or holidays are limited to 10 hours’ pay at the applicable rate plus a sleepover allowance, or can also claim other minimum-rate, penalty, overtime and sleepover entitlements without limitation.

Key holding: A specific enterprise agreement clause governing agreed overnight excursion, camp or client holiday work overrides more general agreement provisions, so the cl 6.11 entitlement of 10 hours at the applicable rate plus a sleepover allowance limits other payments, while the “applicable rate” may itself incorporate penalty or overtime rates.

Applying the well established principle of more specific provisions overriding more broad provisions when they deal with the same subject matter, the entitlements in cl. 6.11 apply when an employee undertakes the work set out in that clause. Employees are not entitled to the payment in cl . 6.11 and a further payment arising from each of the broader agreement provisions.

entry.content:

Key holding: A resignation is a dismissal under s.386(1)(b) only where the employer’s conduct or course of conduct was intended to bring about the resignation or had the probable result that the employee had no effective or real choice but to resign, with employer conduct being essential.

This action is evident in the actions of the Employer, and the intended result of the conduct to bring about the Applicant's resignation; or that that would be the probable result.

entry.title: Kirby and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social Security) [2026] ARTA 2292
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a Centrelink decision raising a $4,109.18 newstart allowance debt against Mr Kirby for 30 November 2018 to 1 April 2019 due to undeclared employment income. The Tribunal set aside the decision and remitted the matter because Centrelink’s earlier income apportionment was not the method required under s 1117D(9) of the Social Security Act 1991. Any recalculated overpayment remains a Commonwealth debt and recovery was not waived.

Key holding: Where pre-7 December 2020 Division 3 work income is reviewed and neither the entitlement period in which it was earned nor the payroll period can be identified, it must be assessed under s 1117D(9) in the entitlement period in which it was received.

This means that the third approach in subsection 1117D(9) must be used so that [Mr Kirby's] wages are to be assessed on each day of the newstart allowance entitlement period in which he received the income.

entry.title: Ms Ashleigh Llewellyn v Sexyland Australia Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 1302 (17 April 2026)
entry.content:
Ms Llewellyn made an unfair dismissal application on 27 August 2025 and then a general protections dismissal application on 2 September 2025. The Commission found the later general protections application was barred by s.725 because the earlier unfair dismissal application had not been withdrawn or failed on specified grounds, and dismissed it under s.587(1)(a).

Key holding: Section 725 prevents an applicant from making a general protections dismissal application while a prior unfair dismissal application in relation to the dismissal remains on foot, and such later application may be dismissed under s.587(1)(a).

As at 2 September 2025 when the general protections application was made, Ms Llewellyn's unfair dismissal application had not been withdrawn, failed for want of jurisdiction, or failed because the Commission found the dismissal to be a genuine redundancy. Ms Llewellyn was, therefore, prevented by section 725 from making a general protections involving dismissal application.

entry.title: Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union v Qube Ports Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 1331 (17 April 2026)
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission dealt with a s.739 dispute between the CFMEU and Qube Ports about whether the Stevedoring Industry Award 2020 prevented Qube from rostering employees who had worked a night shift to an evening shift the next calendar day. Deputy President Dean found the Agreement and Award were inconsistent on shift definitions and minimum breaks, so the Qube Ports Port of Port Kembla Enterprise Agreement 2024 prevailed. The answer to the disputed question was no.

Key holding: Where an enterprise agreement comprehensively regulates shift classifications and minimum breaks and specifically permits rostering that the Award prohibits, the inconsistency is resolved in favour of the Agreement.

The inconsistency is clear, that is the Agreement specifically allows for a rostering arrangement that the Award does not. In those circumstances, the Agreement prevails.
